newsitem.title: USA: New PJM power transmission rates get mixed review.
newsitem.headline: New PJM power transmission rates get mixed review.

text.p: New transmission prices in the Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland (PJM) Interconnect power pool have achieved mixed results since they went into effect April 1, market sources said.
Traders and marketers said the new set of fees, which are generally cheaper than before, have enhanced the liquidity of the most active market in the eastern U.S.
"It appears easier for load serving entities (utilities) to bring power into PJM," a Houston power marketer said.
For example, a New York electric utility bordering PJM now pays less than $1 per megawatt hour in transmission costs versus $3 prior to April 1.

The new PJM transmission prices are part of PJM's overall restructuring to comply with a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) order to open PJM and other power pools' transmission networks for competition.
Industry sources said enthusiasm for the new prices has been dampened by trouble logging on to PJM member websites for transmission data and by new procedures in power scheduling.
"It's cheaper but more complicated," the Houston power marketer said.

In the new competitive environment, utility schedulers no longer have access to valuable information such as hourly updates about the pool's generation costs and operating status of PJM's power plants.
"People are skittish with the new restructuring," said one PJM utility source. "There's no scheduling rate, no load forecast, no peak rates."

Industry sources noted the level of PJM trading has slowed since the implementation of the new transmission prices. Some traders linked the slowdown to a drop in energy demand in the spring rather than the new rates.
"I think it's going to impact how power is going in and out of the pool. If you're selling inside the pool, I don't think you'll be affected," said another PJM power marketer.
During periods of high power demand or generation tightness in PJM, additional transmission fees, also known as congestion charges, will be assessed on electricity being imported into the PJM system.
At the end of March, some PJM participants, notably power marketers, filed complaints with FERC about the new PJM transmission rates.
